title: 9 Personal Project Ideas: Astronomy for MYP Students
summary: Personal Project ideas for astronomy students, with nine practical options, clear learning and product goals, success criteria, and a full MYP example.
body_markdown:
The best Personal Project ideas for astronomy combine a question you care about, something specific to learn, and a product you can realistically create. You do not need an expensive telescope or advanced physics. You need a manageable challenge and evidence showing how your thinking developed.


Astronomy begins with enormous questions. A successful MYP Year 5 project makes one small enough to investigate carefully. The Personal Project includes a process, a product or outcome, and a reflective report. RevisionDojo’s guide to[what the MYP Personal Project involves](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-myp-personal-project) explains how these fit together.


### A quick astronomy project checklist


Before committing, check that you can:


- Explain your personal interest.
- Identify knowledge or skills you need to develop.
- Create a specific product within your timeline.
- Write detailed, testable success criteria.
- Record research, decisions, feedback, and improvements.
- Work safely with available equipment.


Separate what you want to **learn** from what you want to **make** . If those overlap confusingly, use RevisionDojo’s guide to[writing a strong Personal Project goal](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/strong-myp-personal-project-goal) .


### Nine Personal Project ideas for astronomy


Adapt these options to your location, budget, experience, and school deadlines.


Project idea Learning goal Product goal


**Beginner night-sky guide** Understand how seasons, latitude, and light pollution affect visibility. Illustrate a guide to 10-15 objects visible locally.


**Moon observation journal** Understand how lunar orbit relates to phases, position, and rise times. Create a month-long journal with observations, predictions, and explanations.


**Light-pollution investigation** Learn to record sky brightness consistently. Produce a local light-pollution map and awareness campaign.


**Exoplanet transit analysis** Understand how changes in stellar brightness reveal possible transits. Analyse an open dataset and explain an annotated light curve.


**Solar system scale model** Explore planetary sizes, distances, and mathematical scale. Build a physical or digital model documenting calculations and limitations.


**Astrophotography guide** Investigate exposure, focus, stability, noise, and editing. Present an image portfolio and explain tested techniques.


**Constellation stories podcast** Research cultural interpretations of selected star patterns. Compare at least three interpretations in a researched podcast series.


**Mars habitat design** Investigate radiation, temperature, atmosphere, water, and human needs. Create a labelled habitat design with scientific justifications.


**Astronomy learning game** Explore how games explain scientific concepts to younger students. Design, test, and revise a board game or digital prototype.


These are starting points. Strong[MYP Personal Project ideas](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/good-myp-personal-project-topics) become more focused as students consider access, audience, time, and prior knowledge.


Before choosing, run a small feasibility test. Try one observation, open one dataset, or build one game component. Note how long it takes and what prevents progress. For an observation project, plan for cloudy nights and record the conditions alongside each entry. For a design project, identify who can test the prototype. This early trial gives you practical evidence for adjusting your scope before the deadline becomes urgent.


A student announces an ambitious plan to understand the universe before a friend points out the telescope lens cap is still attached.


*A student discovers that exploring the universe sometimes begins with one small practical detail.*


### Turn an astronomy interest into a workable project


Imagine Maya, a hypothetical student interested in exoplanets. Her first idea is a presentation about distant worlds. Research helps her narrow it to transit photometry: measuring the decrease in a star’s brightness when a planet crosses in front of it from our viewpoint.


### Learning and product goals


Her **learning goal** is to understand transit photometry and develop basic data-analysis skills. Her **product goal** is a beginner-friendly digital guide explaining the method through an annotated light curve generated from an open dataset.


NASA’s Exoplanet Watch offers introductory resources and opportunities to analyse existing observations. Access to suitable data makes this project possible without owning a telescope. Before committing, Maya should check that she can obtain, open, and interpret a suitable dataset.


### Testable success criteria


Her guide should:


- Explain transit photometry accurately for readers aged 14-16.
- Include a light curve from an identified dataset.
- Label time, brightness, baseline, and transit dip.
- Explain transit depth and its limitations.
- Define eight relevant scientific terms.
- Cite datasets, images, and scientific sources consistently.
- Document feedback from three target readers and resulting revisions.


She might investigate the approximate relationship between fractional transit depth and the squared ratio of planet radius to star radius. Explaining its assumptions matters as much as presenting the relationship.


The[MYP Personal Project criteria](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-criteria) address planning, applying skills, and reflecting. Specific requirements make evaluation clearer than a criterion such as “looks professional.”


### A realistic action plan


An illustrative nine-week plan could allocate weeks 1-2 to research, weeks 3-4 to practising analysis, and week 5 to interpreting the light curve. Week 6 becomes drafting time; week 7 covers reader feedback and scientific checks. Week 8 allows revision and evaluation, with week 9 reserved for selecting evidence and completing the report.


Build in alternatives. If a dataset proves unsuitable, record why, compare replacements, and explain your decision. That difficulty can become evidence of research and self-management.


### Collect evidence while you work


Keep dated research notes, source evaluations, calculations, drafts, supervisor feedback, unsuccessful tests, and revisions. Select evidence that connects an action to a consequence.


Instead of stating “I used communication skills,” show reader feedback, explain your interpretation, and identify what changed. RevisionDojo’s guide to[avoiding common Personal Project mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-myp-personal-project-mistakes-e0513f75) helps identify gaps before reporting.


Evaluate the finished product against each success criterion separately. If readers misunderstand an axis label, record that finding and revise the explanation. If weather limits your Moon journal, explain how the missing observations affect your conclusions. Distinguish what the product achieved from what you learned while making it. Both deserve specific evidence, including limitations that remain unresolved.


Safety belongs in the plan. Never look at the Sun through a telescope, binoculars, or camera without appropriate solar equipment and informed specialist supervision. Choose lunar observation or open data if safe solar resources are unavailable.


### Choose depth and keep your curiosity


Explore[Personal Project examples for inspiration](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/real-examples-of-ib-myp-personal-projects-for-inspiration) , then check[how the Personal Project is graded](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-is-the-myp-personal-project-graded) . Preserve your own question and decisions.

A focused astronomy project turns curiosity into something you can explain, test, and evaluate.
